title: Organizations That Must Look for Talent From the Outside
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that an organization's forced reliance on outside hiring for senior roles is not neutral bad luck but a diagnostic signal of long-neglected succession planning. The author distinguishes normal, occasional external hires from a pattern of dependency, arguing the latter reveals that developing internal talent through job rotation, coaching, and honest feedback has been deprioritized over a long period. A key argument is that the cost of this neglect compounds silently: a minor early shortfall in succession planning can, left unaddressed, become a full-blown crisis within a decade, forcing rushed, high-stakes external CEO searches at precisely the moments when institutional stability matters most. The piece frames the remedy as straightforward but demanding sustained commitment despite short-term financial pressure — treating leadership capability as an asset that must be deliberately and continuously built through stretch assignments, mentorship, and structured coaching rather than assumed to develop on its own. The essay closes with a statistic meant to sharpen the stakes: roughly 40 percent of externally hired senior leaders fail or materially underperform within their first 18 to 24 months, converting succession planning from a nice-to-have HR function into a direct business risk.
points: Reframes a forced outside CEO search not as neutral circumstance but as a lagging signal that leadership pipeline development has been deprioritized or ignored over a long period.

Argues succession-planning neglect compounds silently: a minor early shortfall can, left unaddressed for a decade, escalate into a full-blown crisis forcing rushed external searches at the worst possible moments.

Insists leadership capability must be treated as an organizational asset built deliberately through stretch assignments, mentorship, honest feedback, and structured coaching, not assumed to emerge naturally.

Cites a specific failure-rate statistic, roughly 40 percent of externally hired senior leaders underperforming within 18-24 months, to convert succession planning from an HR nicety into a quantified business risk.

Frames the ability to promote from within as one of the clearest indicators of organizational health, arguing pipeline-strong organizations become talent magnets while pipeline-weak ones pay a permanent premium in the external market.
quotes: While circumstances can occur that dash well-laid plans, having to hire an outside CEO is a signal that developing the leadership pipeline has been a low priority or ignored over a long period of time.

What begins as a minor shortfall in succession planning can, within a decade, become a full-blown crisis. This forces boards and decision-makers into rushed, high-stakes external searches at the exact moments when stability and institutional knowledge matter most.

That means dedicating real resources to stretch assignments, mentorship, honest performance feedback, and structured coaching. Leadership capability, like any other organizational asset, must be built deliberately and continuously.

Organizations that excel at leadership development also become magnets for talent. Those that neglect the work of talent development find themselves at the mercy of the external marketplace, where they must pay a premium for talent they could have grown themselves.

Given that roughly 40 percent of all externally hired senior leaders fail or materially underperform within the first 18-24 months, creating a strong talent pipeline is not just a leadership imperative. It is a business imperative.
